1.2 MSI file structure, storage, and basic navigation

1.2.1 Home directory - Tier 1 storage?
Once you are in, you will be in your default directory, which is (I believe) also your Tier 1 storage. As group PI, I currently have 1Tb of storage allotted for the entire group, and if you are one of my group members, you will be counting towards that total. To check where you are, just print working directory:
pwd
My home directory is “/users/2/jeli0026”.


1.2.2 Scratch - local and global?
what is the difference? and how much storage #to-do - note I should make a table about this


1.2.3 Tier 2 Storage
Unclear the use case for this, but here is the documentation: MSI data retention and protection. Tier 2 is object storage (like Amazon or S3). You can use Globus to move data from your Tier 2 into your home directory (Tier 1) or into global scratch.
https://msi.umn.edu/about-msi-services/data-storage/second-tier-storage https://msi.umn.edu/our-resources/knowledge-base/data-storage-faqs/how-do-i-use-globus-transfer-data-second-tier-storage-msi
Everyone has 120Tb of storage at Tier 2.


1.2.4 Basic navigation
You can do basic navigation of files and folders using the command line, for example listing all files and folders in a directory:
ls -a
Or if you want to see the file size in megabytes for all files in a directory:
ls -l --block-size=MB
Or changing directories - to go up:

cd ..
To change directories within an existing directory:

cd newdirectory
…where newdirectory is the directory name you would like to change to. Al lot more basic commands in the Software Carpentry cheatsheet here.

title: 2  Accessing and Utilizing Storage on MSI Systems
text:
2.1 Tier 1 Storage
Tier 1 storage is the default home directory and group storage on MSI and is equivalent to High Performance Storage. Any files (objects) stored in the following locations (I’m using my x500 here just as an example) are on Tier 1 storage:
/users/2/jeli0026 - private storage
/home/jeli0026/shared - shared with lab group members. accessed by typing “shared” when in the home directory
/home/jeli0026/public - accessible by all MSI users. accessed by typing “public” when in the home directory
The default for Tier 1 storage is 150Gb. Group PIs can request more (up to 20Tb). I have currently requested and received 1Tb of storage on Tier 1 (as of 17OCT2024). All of the Tier one storage used by my group members also counts towards this quota.
crumbs: 2  Accessing and Utilizing Storage on MSI Systems

title: 2  Accessing and Utilizing Storage on MSI Systems
text:
2.2 Scatch Storage
Scratch storage is also High Performance Storage, but does not count against the PI group Tier 1 quota. Each user is allocated 40Tb on scratch storage. HOWEVER - scratch storage is not backed up and may be deleted after 30 days. SO scratch storage should only be used for active processes - there should always be copies of data on scratch storage elsewhere. ALSO< scratch storage is by default private storage to the user (no shared permissions). There are two options for scratch storage:
/scratch.global - this storage is accessible by all nodes - this should be the default use case for scratch storage. Users must make a directory for themselves when using global scratch (e.g. mkdir /scratch.global/$USER). Where $USER should be your x500 - then in that case, your global scratch is at /scratch.global/jeli0026 for example. You can access scratch.global by typing “scratch.global” or “scratch”
/scratch.local - this storage is only accessible by a single node. You can access scratch.local by typing “scratch.local”.
From Google AI generated search: The main difference between global scratch and local scratch at the Minnesota Supercomputing Institute (MSI) is that global scratch is shared and visible to all nodes, while local scratch is only connected to a single node:
Global scratch
A shared space with a 40 TB and 10 million file quota. Users must create a directory for themselves when using global scratch.
Local scratch
A disk, SSD, or RAMdisk that is only visible and connected to a single node.
Here are some other things to know about scratch storage at MSI:
Scratch storage is temporary and should not be used for data that is valuable or needs to be stored for more than 30 days. There is no backup or snapshots for local or global scratch storage. Access to scratch storage is requested like processors, memory, and GPUs. The amount of free capacity for each scratch type varies based on how much the shared resources are being used. Users can only transfer data for which they have normal filesystem read access. Users can only place new data in directories for which they have normal filesystem write access.
crumbs: 2  Accessing and Utilizing Storage on MSI Systems

title: 2  Accessing and Utilizing Storage on MSI Systems
text:
2.3 Tier 2 Storage
MSI Tier 2 Storage is completely separate from Tier 1 and is an S3 bucket based system that you can access either from the command line or from Globus. Accessibility from the command line uses the s3cmd tool at MSI. All users have allocated 40Tb of storage on the Tier 2 system. Notably, the Tier 2 system is S3 storage buckets - you can set permissions to allow others to access.
From that documentation, you can create your own bucket as follows:
To create your own bucket (AKA folder) on s3.msi.umn.edu, you can use the “mb” command (make bucket):
s3cmd mb s3://mynewbucket

title: 5  Transferring data from a Google Cloud Bucket to MSI
text:
5.2 Initiating File Transfers
Now, gcloud CLI is installed in my global scratch and I can use the tools to transfer fiels from any Google Cloud s3 buckets I have access to (via my google account) to my global scratch.

Initiate login authorization:

gcloud auth login
This resulted in the following:
Go to the following link in your browser, and complete the sign-in prompts:
    https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?response_type=code&client_id=32555940559.apps.googleusercontent.com&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fsdk.cloud.google.com%2Fauthcode.html&scope=openid+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Fuserinfo.email+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Fcloud-platform+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Fappengine.admin+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Fsqlservice.login+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Fcompute+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.googleapis.com%2Fauth%2Faccounts.reauth&state=UfyB6sxKehakuKWy0psVzx2AMkQaRx&prompt=consent&token_usage=remote&access_type=offline&code_challenge=VFldrf31Ur1fgqlo8IiRP01UwIIhoyN6UuKFi8ZfPmg&code_challenge_method=xxxx

Once finished, enter the verification code provided in your browser: 
I copied and pasted the link into my browser (you will have a different link) and was prompted to sign in using my google account. After that I received a verification code. I then copied and pasted that verification code into the terminal prompt.
I then received this message:
You are now logged in as [jeli0026@umn.edu].
Your current project is [None].  You can change this setting by running:
  $ gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID
In this case I think it is telling me how to navigate to one of the buckets I have access to.

Navigating to bucket and inspecting structure/objects

Here is how I listed all the files in Timm’s akveg-map Google Cloud bucket:
gsutil ls gs://akveg-data/
NOTE: although on Google Cloud Console this bucket is called akveg-map, it appears that the actual name is akveg-data because akveg-map comes back as not found, but akveg-data is correct. You can verify that what you are seeing on the command line listing is correct by navigating to the web user interface for Google Cloud Console (https://console.cloud.google.com). Any organizations you have access to should be available in the pull down menu. You can then go to the hamburger menu on the left and navigate to cloud storage. From there you can use the user interface links to navigate through the directories and inspect the files. PS NOTE: Ah I see - the ORGANIZATION is called akveg-map, but the bucket itself currently housing the covariates is called akveg-data.
If I want to inspect a subdirectory, for example, I would just do this:
gsutil ls gs://akveg-data/covariates_v20240711/

Using rsync to transfer files.

Now we are going to use the gsutil tool rsync to transfer files. rsync is a “recursive” syncing utility. In this case recursive syncing means it can process all files and subdirectories in a given directory (instead of just the contents of the directory itself without subdirectories). rsync is a one way syncing from source to destination. The advantage of rsync utility rather than copy (cp) is that rsync will look for what is already in the destination directory and only copy what isn’t there (so if there are new files you don’t need to re-transfer everything).
gsutil -m rsync -r gs://akveg-data/covariates_v20240711/ /scratch.global/jeli0026
NOTE: In the gsutil command you provided, the flags -m and -r have the following meanings:
-m (multi-threaded/multi-processing): This flag tells gsutil to perform operations in parallel, meaning it can transfer multiple files simultaneously. This increases performance, especially for large datasets or directories with many files.
-r (recursive): This flag tells gsutil to operate recursively, meaning it will process all files and subdirectories within the specified directory.
ADDITIONAL NOTE: There are two arguments that must be in this order: SOURCE and DESTINATION
This will transfer all data from the specified bucket and directory to the destination directory!

title: 5  Transferring data from a Google Cloud Bucket to MSI
section: 5.3 Transferring data from scratch.global to MSI Tier 2
text:
5.3 Transferring data from scratch.global to MSI Tier 2
Since everything on scratch.global is private, I need to transfer to MSI Tier 2 to make this data available to others. First I need to make a bucket on MSI Tier 2 and set permissions. Then I will transfer the data into my bucket.

First, since when I did the file transfer it dumped all files straight into my global scratch I’m going to make a directory to house then. NOTE: you can avoid this in the future by making a directory within scratch and setting that as your destination.

mkdir covariates_v20240711

Now transfer all files with .tif extension into that folder:

mv *.tif /scratch.global/jeli0026/covariates_v20240711

Now use the Tier 2 s3cmd tool instructions to create a new bucket on Tier 2 called aksdb_covars:

s3cmd mb s3://aksdb-covars
NOTE: The bucket name can be between 3 and 63 characters long, and can contain only lower-case characters, numbers, periods, and dashes.
Success!:
Bucket 's3://aksdb-covars/' created

Now use the sync tool to copy files into the bucket:

s3cmd sync ./covariates_v20240711 s3://aksdb-covars
NOTE: should run this command from the higher level directory that your fiels are in (so in other words I should be in scratch.global/jeli0026 when I run the command). NOTE actually this should work fine with the ‘.’. I was trying before with the ‘~’ and this by default points to the home directory. You can also use the tilda to navigate directly to your home directory!!!!
ADDITIONAL NOTE: yes this worked fine - you can really be from any directory. So: this would have worked fine too (or any adjusted version):
s3cmd sync ~/scratch.global/jeli0026/covariates_v20240711 s3://aksdb-covars

Set open permissions for the bucket so others can access it:

To recursively make a bucket and all its contents publically readable by everyone:
s3cmd setacl -P -r s3://aksdb-covars

Additional s3cmd tools

Note that you can find additional documentation for s3cmd here: https://s3tools.org/usage

title: 6  Working with Docker Images on MSI Resources
text:
6.1 Singularity in place of docker
Due to security concerns, MSI does not allow direct import and use of Docker images. Instead, you need to use Singularity, which, like docker, has a repository of images that can be accessed. These are .SIF files. You can build a .sif from an existing docker image, however. Then you can store it in your home directory.
I used the “Singularity and Containers” tutorial (from 2020) to do this. There may be some outdated issues but it seemed to generally work.
crumbs: 6  Working with Docker Images on MSI Resources
